extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/aesthetics; artists, composers, critics interested in theory of tragedy and music
extracted.subtask_short: aesthetic theory of tragedy and music
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative standards and compositional guidance from a philosophical treatment of the fine arts, focusing on what makes tragedy and music effective and how they relate to the will/idea. Useful for critics, composers, dramatists, and students of aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential element of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The representation of a great misfortune is alone essential to tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy must present a substantial misfortune; mere incident or moral lesson is insufficient. The poet's task is to bring a great catastrophe into view so that the æsthetic effect of tragedy can occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three specific ways to introduce tragic misfortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Misfortune may be introduced (1) by a character of extraordinary wickedness, (2) through blind fate (chance and error), or (3) by the mere position/relations of the dramatis personæ with regard to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (1) Richard III, Iago, Shylock, Franz Moor, Phaedra, Creon; (2) Oedipus Rex, Trachiniae, many ancient tragedies, Romeo and Juliet among moderns; (3) tragedies where ordinary characters' relations compel tragic injury, e.g., Clavigo (model), Hamlet (partly), Wallenstein, Faust (Gretchen episodes), Corneille's Cid (lacking tragic conclusion). Use these categories when analyzing how the catastrophe arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority of relational/position-based tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The misfortune arising from the position and relations of ordinary characters (the third kind) surpasses the other two, because it makes the greatest misfortune seem near and essential to human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer tragic designs where ordinary characters, not monstrous wickedness or prodigious fate, produce the catastrophe through their positions and relations. This creates stronger identification and horror since such entanglements could be ours; it requires achieving great effect with minimal causes—thus is more difficult and artistically valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic purification by suffering and renunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy often culminates in the hero's purified resignation: after long conflict and suffering the noblest men renounce ends and pleasures, or surrender life, their will to live being 'dead' and replaced by knowledge that quiets the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The climax of effective tragedy is not mere punishment but the hero's insight and renunciation—examples: Calderon's steadfast prince, Gretchen in Faust, Hamlet, Joan of Arc, Maid of Orleans. Critically, the tragic ending should present purification through suffering rather than simplistic moral retribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of poetical justice as a requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The demand for poetical justice (that evildoers be punished and good rewarded) rests on a misconception of tragedy and the world; absence of poetical justice is appropriate and realistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not impose moralistic expectations (poetical justice) on tragic works; the absence of clear moral retribution may be disturbing but is truer to tragedy's insight that existence itself (original sin) is at issue. Criticism that laments lack of poetical justice (e.g., Samuel Johnson's complaints) misunderstands tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music's singular status among the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Music stands alone, cut off from the other arts: it does not represent Ideas via particular things but is a direct objectification and copy of the will itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat music as uniquely capable of expressing the in-itself (will) rather than phenomena or ideas. Its effect is stronger, quicker, and more necessary than other arts; analysis of music must account for its directness and metaphysical role rather than forcing analogies to pictorial representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music should express universals, not particular events
rubrics_metrics.description: Music never expresses particular definite joys, sorrows, or events themselves, but the essential nature of joy, sorrow, pain, delight, etc., in the abstract—the in-itself of these states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compositions meant to capture universal feeling (melody) should avoid tying themselves too closely to specific narrative events. The music's power lies in its universality; audiences readily seek to give it concrete form, but the music's proper domain is the quintessence of feeling without motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of words to music; avoid music serving merely words
rubrics_metrics.description: The text of a song or opera should remain subordinate; it is a great misconception and perversity when text becomes chief and music only a means of expressing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In setting words to music, ensure the music retains its independent, universal expressive power. Rossini praised as an example whose music 'speaks its own language' and is effective without words. Beware of operatic/textual practices that make music merely illustrative of narrative events—which is a misapplication of music's nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody as work of genius and inspiration, not conscious concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The composition of melody—the disclosure of deepest secrets of human willing and feeling—is the work of genius, lying far from reflection and conscious intention; melody often arises from inspiration rather than conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composers should cultivate receptive, inspired creation rather than strictly deliberate conceptual construction. The composer's 'man' is separated from the artist: the artist composes by inspiration, revealing inner nature beyond reason's comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence of musical strata to grades of being (bass/harmony/melody)
rubrics_metrics.description: In analogy: the deep bass corresponds to unorganised nature (mass of planet); complemental harmonic parts correspond to lower grades (plants, beasts); the high singing melody corresponds to the intellectual life of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or analyzing, consider roles: bass should move slowly and represent the lowest grades; accompaniment/harmony supply gradations; melody provides connected, significant progression reflecting intellect. Full effect requires the integration of all voices (melody with accompaniment down to bass) to mirror the object's full gradation of will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melodic motion as expression of will's striving and satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody's constant deviation from and return to the keynote mirrors the will's quick transition from wish to satisfaction; quick melodies without great deviations are cheerful, slow melodies with painful discords express sadness; minor vs major conveys pain vs relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tonal movement, deviations, returns, tempo, and modality to mirror psychological states: Allegro maestoso for noble striving toward distant ends; Adagio for great painful effort; minor mode for anxious/painful feeling, major for release. The structure of melody should embody 'effort and satisfaction' sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid specially imitative (programmatic) music
rubrics_metrics.description: Specially imitative music that directly imitates external phenomena (e.g., Haydn's 'The Seasons', passages of 'The Creation', battle-pieces) gives only an inadequate imitation of phenomena and is to be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of music that merely mimics natural or narrative events; such direct imitation reduces music to phenomenon imitation instead of expressing the will itself. Programmatic tricks that literalize sounds into pictured events undermine music's metaphysical universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music's seriousness and appropriate use of repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Music's object is the will (the most serious of things), so absurdity is excluded from its peculiar province; repetitions (including Da capo) that would be unbearable in words are appropriate in music and useful for deep comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect music's seriousness; avoid trivializing it. Use repetition purposefully: musical reprises can enhance understanding and aesthetic effect in ways unavailable to verbal art. Recognize music's distinct rhetorical resources and do not force linguistic norms onto it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of inherent musical imperfection (temperament)
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfectly accurate, pure system of music is arithmetically impossible (irrationalities in ratios); therefore all music deviates from absolute purity and uses temperament to conceal necessary discords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composers, theorists, and instrument-makers should accept temperament and the impossibility of absolute purity; practical tuning systems and distribution of slight impure intervals are necessary artistic/physical realities rather than flaws to be eliminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: To grasp theoretical analogies, listen reflectively and be system-familiar
rubrics_metrics.description: To assent to and understand the exposition of music's inner nature, one should often listen to music with constant reflection upon the theory and be very familiar with the whole system of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars and critics should pair attentive, repeated listening with familiarity of the broader theoretical system to evaluate and comprehend music's metaphysical claims; isolated or casual listening will not reveal the analogies described.
